 By Faithlyn Graham

 Morrisey administration addresses how recently proposed cuts to SNAP may impact West Virginians. 
 CHARLESTON, W.Va. — Gov. Patrick Morrisey's administration says a proposed federal rule tightening eligibility requirements for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program would not directly affect West Virginia's Temporary Assistance for Needy Families funding or eligibility requirements, though some households could lose access to food assistance.
 In a response to questions from WV News, the governor's team said, “The proposed federal rule does not change eligibility for West Virginia's TANF program or reduce federal TANF funding.”
 The Trump administration recently proposed eliminating a policy that allows states to automatically extend SNAP eligibility to certain households receiving assistance through the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program, commonly known as TANF.
 The proposed rule would narrow broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), a policy that allows states to extend SNAP eligibility to households receiving certain noncash benefits through TANF-funded programs, even if they exceed standard federal income or resource limits.
 Under regular SNAP eligibility rules, most households must have a gross income at or below 130% of the federal poverty guidelines. However, states using BBCE can raise that threshold to as much as 200% of the guidelines and increase or eliminate asset limits.
 If finalized, the rule would limit categorical eligibility through TANF to households that qualify for direct TANF assistance, rather than those receiving noncash or in-kind services. More households would have to undergo federal income and resource assessments to determine whether they qualify for SNAP.
 The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates the proposed change could result in approximately 6.3 million Americans losing SNAP benefits, with the changes projected to take full effect in fiscal year 2029. In West Virginia, approximately 272,800 residents receive SNAP benefits each month.
 The Morrisey administration said the proposal would primarily affect households receiving TANF-funded informational benefits rather than direct cash assistance.
 “Families receiving WV WORKS cash assistance would retain their categorical eligibility for SNAP,” the governor's team said.
 Informational benefits can include resources such as informational pamphlets or telephone hotlines that help families locate available services, according to the USDA.
 Under current policy, receiving even these nominal benefits can allow a household to qualify for SNAP through broad-based categorical eligibility without meeting the program's standard federal income and resource requirements.
 However, households qualifying through other TANF-funded benefits could face additional requirements.
 “Those households would need to meet regular federal SNAP income and asset requirements to continue receiving benefits,” the administration said.
 The proposal comes as West Virginia faces separate concerns about the sustainability of its TANF program, which supports a range of services for low-income families, including child care assistance, Family Support Centers, school clothing vouchers, foster care and adoption services.
 A recent analysis from the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy found TANF spending increased by 51%, or approximately $61 million, between 2023 and 2025. During that period, the state's TANF reserve declined from $142 million to approximately $83 million.
 The center estimated the reserve could be exhausted by the end of federal fiscal year 2027, based on available spending trends.
 Asked whether the proposed SNAP changes could place additional strain on TANF or other state-funded assistance programs, the administration said West Virginia would continue supporting families through existing programs.
 “West Virginia will continue providing assistance to eligible families through its existing programs,” the governor's team said.
 The administration added that the Department of Human Services would make necessary administrative adjustments.
 “The Department of Human Services will address any additional administrative needs as the federal requirements are finalized,” the response said.
 The governor's team did not directly state whether Morrisey supports the proposed federal rule.
 “The administration's focus is on ensuring West Virginia families have access to the assistance programs for which they qualify and that any federal changes are implemented effectively,” the response said.
 The Department of Human Services expects to submit comments on the proposed rule before the Dec. 10 deadline.
 WV News also contacted the Department of Human Services for additional information about the potential effects of the proposal on West Virginia's assistance programs but had not received a response as of publication.
